output.headline: Clean energy investment doubles that of fossil fuels, analysis finds
output.bodyHtml:
Clean energy investment is now double that of fossil fuels, electric car use is soaring, deforestation of the Amazon in Brazil has fallen sharply and carbon pollution is set to dip slightly this year – causes for optimism, according to Climate Action Tracker (CAT), even though the world is still failing to cut emissions in line with the science and countries’ own promises.

The report by Climate Action Tracker (CAT) found that, under current policies, the planet will heat up by 2.7C on average by the end of the century compared with preindustrial times – up slightly from a prediction of 2.6C in the group’s analysis conducted last year.

The analysis found that the world is heading for an “irrecoverable overshoot” of global temperature thresholds that will plunge billions of people into disastrous climate impacts, because governments have stalled for so long to cut planet-heating emissions.

This level of warming smashes the 1.5C threshold that was agreed by countries a decade ago but is set to be breached in just a few years. Scientists have warned that beyond this point already harmful storms, droughts, heatwaves, flooding and other impacts will become intolerable for parts of the world and potentially trigger runaway climate change that won’t be contained.

Related: ‘My classroom was 30C. No one was learning. Then I started to feel dizzy’ – This is climate breakdown

The UN secretary-general, António Guterres, said on Tuesday that this reality should compel governments to act quickly to phase out the fossil fuels that are causing the climate crisis, as countries, minus the US, gathered in the Turkish city of Antalya for UN climate talks that have centred on the looming “overshoot” of the temperature target.

If countries did act decisively to slash emissions then the future temperature projections would become less daunting, the CAT report states. However, in even the most optimistic scenario – where all pledges, targets and other long-term promises made by countries were fulfilled – the world would still heat up by 1.9C by the end of the century.

Such targets have been routinely flouted by the countries that have made them, however. This means leaders face a crunch moment, experts say.

Bill Hare, chief executive of CAT partner organisation Climate Analytics, says: “The stark choice for governments is to either continue to support the fossil fuel industry, which would consign humanity to insurmountable economic damages, rising mortality from heat and climate-driven diseases and disasters that they are unable to adapt to – or pivot to the solutions which are available and cheaper than ever.”

Hare said exceeding 1.5C warming “cannot be an excuse to open the door to defeatism” and that every small increment of temperature rise will be significant. The CAT analysis is similar to one recently put out by the UN, which uses previous CAT data to inform its own projections.

Related: National security of all countries at risk due to climate crisis, UK foreign secretary warns

Greta Thunberg, the Swedish climate advocate, arrived in Antalya on Tuesday and warned that “everything and everyone we love is at stake” because of the failure to confront the climate crisis, even as more will need to be done to avert disastrous climate impacts.

“Governments collectively are simply not moving fast enough to adopt the policies that would enable us to escape from the emerging overshoot trap,” said Sarah Heck, lead author of the CAT report. Some countries, such as the US, Canada and New Zealand, are even slowing down their climate action to a “staggering level”, she added.
output.standfirst: Clean energy investment is now double that of fossil fuels, analysis finds, even as the world is told it risks an 'irrecoverable overshoot' that would 'consign humanity to disasters they are unable to adapt to'.
output.progress: UN secretary-general António Guterres says the findings should spur governments to act quickly and phase out fossil fuels.

output.headline: Police watchdog calls for stronger safeguards on facial recognition technology
output.bodyHtml:
Britain’s police watchdog has called for a clearer statutory framework, stronger national standards and improved oversight of facial recognition technology, after an inspection found that errors and bias in the systems risk the wrongful arrest of innocent people, especially those from ethnic minorities.

The report by His Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary, published on Wednesday, covers only retrospective facial recognition. The technology is seen as less controversial and less tricky to get right than live facial recognition, which is used in real time to find suspects.

His Majesty’s Inspector of Constabulary Kathryn Stone said continued public support relied on showing the technology was being used properly: “Police forces must be able to show that appropriate safeguards are in place, risks relating to bias and data retention are effectively managed, and decisions are still subject to human judgment. A clearer statutory framework, stronger national standards and improved governance and oversight arrangements are essential to maintaining public confidence.”

Although the technology can help fight crime, the report found it is beset by errors and biases, and operators do not always realise they must make further inquiries to verify the data.

“Some investigators didn’t know that RFR results were intelligence rather than evidence and required further enquiries before officers took enforcement action,” the report said.

“This creates a risk that people could be incorrectly identified or arrested, which could undermine public confidence in the technology.

“We found that some investigators didn’t always carry out enough corroborative enquiries before acting on potential matches. In a small number of cases, officers relied too heavily on RFR results, which led to inappropriate investigative action.”

The report said there are still issues with bias in the algorithm, including being more likely to wrongly flag people from ethnic minorities as suspects.

It said: “More needs to be done to reduce the risks of people being wrongly arrested … Auditors also identified cases where users uploaded poor-quality or unsuitable probe images, including blurred images and images containing multiple faces. These factors reduced the system’s ability to return reliable matches.”

Inspectors also found a risk of public confidence being undermined because custody images that should have been deleted were in fact kept.

The report says: “Inspectors found that legislation hasn’t kept up with changes in facial recognition technology and there is no comprehensive statutory framework governing this technology’s use. This makes it more difficult for forces to understand the lawful basis for RFR’s use and what safeguards are needed to protect the public.”

Facial recognition is seen by police chiefs as the next big leap forward in crime fighting, and next huge threat to civil liberties by sceptics.

Ben Russell, lead on facial recognition for the National Police Chiefs’ Council, said: “Policing remains committed to the ethical, proportionate and responsible use of retrospective facial recognition to help investigate crime, bring offenders to justice and keep communities safe and we are pleased that HMICFRS has recognised the exciting possibilities of this technology.”

Jasleen Chaggar, from Big Brother Watch, said: “The revelations that officers are treating facial recognition as bona fide evidence rather than a probability score is alarming.

“This approach significantly increases the risk that more innocent people will have officers knock on their door to arrest them for crimes committed in towns they’ve never visited, as we’ve seen before.

“Worse still, police aren’t even logging their use of retrospective facial recognition, meaning people could wrongfully become suspects in criminal investigations without even realising why they’ve been accused.

“Police cannot be allowed to continue using the algorithm with so few safeguards and at biased settings that are more likely to misidentify women, Asian and black people and search against millions of unlawfully held custody images.”

Prof Pete Fussey of the University of Southampton, formerly a police adviser on facial recognition, said: “Meaningful human scrutiny of AI systems is a legal requirement, yet the report gives examples of investigators taking the computer’s suggestions at face value without further checks.”
output.standfirst: His Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary says a clearer statutory framework and stronger standards are needed, after finding facial recognition errors and bias risk the wrongful arrest of innocent people, particularly ethnic minorities
output.progress: His Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary has recommended a clearer statutory framework, stronger national standards and improved oversight of the technology.

output.headline: Scott Colom becomes first Black senator popularly elected in Mississippi's history
output.bodyHtml:
Democrat Scott Colom has defeated Cindy Hyde-Smith, the incumbent Republican senator, to become the first Black senator in Mississippi elected since Reconstruction, in a stunning upset after more than a week of vote counting in one of the country’s most reliably red states.

“For me, this journey started with a prayer, y’all,” Colom said while addressing supporters Wednesday night in Jackson, Mississippi. “And in Mississippi, our prayers have often changed the course of history.”

Colom opened up a narrow lead over Hyde-Smith late on election night. His lead widened as election officials counted absentee and provisional ballots. The Associated Press called the contest on Wednesday, after it was clear Hyde-Smith was not able to close the gap.

In a two-minute concession video shared on social media, Hyde-Smith said: “While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters.” She offered her congratulations to Colom and said she wished him well “as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state”.

Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982. It’s been much longer – not since 1875 – that the state sent a Black senator to Washington. Colom is also the first Black man popularly elected to the Senate in the state’s history – during Reconstruction, senators were chosen by state lawmakers.

With Colom’s election, Mississippi, the first state to send Black lawmakers to Congress, has sent more Black people to the Senate than any other state besides Illinois. Blanche K Bruce, the last Black man elected to the Senate from Mississippi, was born into slavery; John C Stennis, the last Democrat to be sent from Mississippi, was, for most of his career, a staunch segregationist.

Colom’s election capped a national wave of anger at Donald Trump’s administration, sweeping away Republicans in places where Democrats hadn’t been competitive in decades. With the addition of Colom, Democrats will hold at least 55 seats in the Senate – the party’s largest midterm gain since 1986.

Across the south, voters were further motivated by the president’s attempt to drastically redraw Black majority districts, attempting to dilute the largely Democratic voting blocs.

Colom has a track record of success in the state. In 2015, Colom unseated a nearly 30-year incumbent when he was elected the first Black district attorney for the 16th circuit. As district attorney, he had a 94 per cent success rate for convictions. He’s a seventh-generation Mississippian, whose father was a longtime Republican who campaigned for Ronald Reagan and was friendly with Thad Cochran, a longtime state politician who resigned from his US Senate seat in 2018 due to declining health.

A string of Democratic stars visited the state late in the race as the polls showed a tightening race – Cory Booker, Pete Buttigieg, Kamala Harris and Bill Clinton all made appearances for Colom. Trump rallied for Hyde-Smith last month.

Joe Biden nominated Colom to be a federal judge in the northern district of Mississippi. With support from both Republicans and Democrats, he appeared to be on track to a lifetime appointment on the federal bench, when Hyde-Smith blocked him from having a confirmation hearing.

“I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being a US senator,” Hyde-Smith said in remarks to supporters on election day.

In the days after the election, as Colom’s vote-margin inched higher, he kept a dizzying campaign pace, visiting Millsaps College, his alma mater, and local colleges Jackson State University and Tougaloo College. With national and international cameras on him, Colom stopped by small, local businesses, including Marshall’s Music and Book Store and OffBeat, both of which are Black-owned, and Brent’s Drugs, a Jackson classic.

Colom campaigned on the promise that “Mississippi matters”. He told voters that he would represent all Mississippians, even those who supported his opponent – and the president.

A week before the vote, he attended Trump’s rally for Hyde-Smith in Corinth to engage the president’s supporters and listen to their economic concerns. He posed for photos with some rally-goers, as they talked to him about high gas prices, grocery bills and health insurance. He later said the face-to-face conversations helped him convert the unlikeliest of voters to his campaign.

Colom drew national attention for a viral ad that played on his opponent’s response to a question about the rising cost of beef: “You have so many proteins to choose from,” Hyde-Smith told a local television host during the interview. Colom’s campaign seized on the moment, producing a 30-second ad that jumps from her reply to a man grilling beef patties. “Pick another protein?” the man says. “Shiiiit. I’d rather pick another senator instead.”

Colom drove a “pick your protein” taco truck around the state, handing out free tacos to voters.

As the days-long counting process commenced, both Hyde-Smith and Colom projected confidence that they would prevail.

National voting groups and attorneys descended upon the Magnolia state, joining the local groups that worked to mobilize voters. Democratic and Republican groups, including the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) and Democratic election attorneys from the Elias Law Group, have deployed hundreds of volunteers and lawyers to all the state’s 82 counties to oversee the final rounds of counting.

Mississippi has no automatic recount law. A recount can only happen if ordered by a court in response to a lawsuit against a county or county election commission from a political party or campaign. Mississippi law does not establish a system for challenging ballots on a statewide scale, so the process would have to be on a county-by-county basis.

“I assure you,” Hyde-Smith said on election night, “I will continue to be your US senator.”

Asked about those comments at a press conference the next day, Colom replied: “Bless her heart.”
output.standfirst: Colom's win, by a razor-thin margin after more than a week of counting, makes him the first Black man popularly elected to the US Senate in Mississippi's history and ends Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith's tenure in one of the country's most reliably red states
output.progress: Colom has pledged to represent all Mississippians, including those who backed his opponent and the president.

output.headline: Nuttall takes charge of vetting as Reform names interim general secretary
output.bodyHtml:
Candidate vetting at Reform is now run by Paul Nuttall, the party’s deputy chair and a former Ukip leader, after the recent case of Madgwick once again brought the process into the spotlight and severely embarrassed the party; Waterhouse’s departure reflects continuing organisational turmoil at Reform.

A Reform UK spokesperson said: “Tom Waterhouse has left his role with Reform UK. The party leader has now appointed an interim general secretary.”

Nigel Farage’s party continues to face turmoil over questions about vetting failures and professionalisation after Reform UK’s general secretary left the role.

The departure of Tom Waterhouse comes after Reform UK’s leader on Hampshire county council, George Madgwick, was charged with 12 counts of rape and one of distributing indecent images of a child.

Waterhouse, a public affairs executive who previously worked in the world of Westminster thinktanks and for the crown estate, was recruited in August last year. Labour described him as Reform’s “latest fall guy” for problems in the party.

Waterhouse’s departure will be a blow to Reform’s drive towards professionalisation, a project of which he had been at the centre. He had been involved in a big recruitment push, bankrolled by wealthy donors, and in the selection of candidates for a future general election.

Waterhouse had also been involved in Reform’s internal investigation into two of its senior officials, James Orr and Dan Jukes, alongside Adam Richardson, the party’s legal secretary and a longstanding associate of Farage. Their investigation cleared Orr and Jukes of breaking laws that ban foreign donations, despite the matter remaining under police investigation.

Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said: “As the scandals pile up for Reform, everyone is being forced to take the blame except Nigel Farage. Their general secretary is the latest fall guy, but we all know nobody in Reform makes a decision without Farage’s approval.

“Farage is yet to come clean on what he knew about the arrest of his senior campaign manager and leader in Hampshire, who is now facing 35 very serious charges. And he tried to cover up a secret £5m ‘gift’ from a crypto billionaire.”

Related: For Trump, Musk and Farage, the message is the same: voters don’t want to be hijacked by billionaires | Rafael Behr

The Reform leader has not concealed his unhappiness at continued failures in candidate vetting and other matters. “I wasn’t very happy,” Farage said when asked why Madgwick, who was arrested in January over several alleged sexual offences, was still in his role nearly 10 months later. Madgwick denies any wrongdoing.

Farage last month blamed “staff incompetence” for a poor turnout and a half-empty hall during a Reform UK economic policy launch event in London.

Staff at Reform’s Millbank HQ were informed on Wednesday that Waterhouse was leaving. He is one of a number of figures seen as an asset to Reform’s push for power who have recently parted ways with the party or been sidelined.

Tim Montgomerie, a high-profile activist who defected from the Conservatives, was suspended in August after he criticised Farage’s decision not to attend the count when he won the Clacton byelection.
output.standfirst: Paul Nuttall now oversees Reform's candidate vetting as the party names an interim general secretary following Tom Waterhouse's departure, amid continued fallout including the case of councillor George Madgwick, charged with 12 counts of rape.
output.progress: Nuttall takes over after Reform's internal inquiry cleared two senior officials of breaking foreign-donation rules, even as that case stays under police investigation.

output.headline: Government presses ahead with bill to outlaw LGBT+ conversion practices
output.bodyHtml:
A draft bill to ban LGBT+ conversion practices, published in June and now open for consultation, sets out potential jail sentences of up to five years for attempts to change someone’s sexual orientation or gender identity that are abusive and cause serious harm.

As equalities minister under previous Conservative governments, Kemi Badenoch supported the idea of a legal ban on conversion practices, saying in 2021 that she wanted to give people ‘the freedom to live their life as they see fit without fear or intimidation’.

Kemi Badenoch has ‘no interest in supporting LGBT+ people’ or promoting tolerance more widely, a government minister has said, after the Conservatives dropped support for a planned law to ban conversion practices.

The comments by Bridget Phillipson, the equalities minister, come after the Tories removed their previous backing for a law targeting abusive practices that aim to change someone’s sexual orientation or gender identity.

Badenoch’s party says this is because of concerns about the scope of the bill, particularly the way it deals with gender identity.

Asked about the bill last week, Badenoch said it would ‘mean that parents start getting arrested for parenting their children’, agreeing with a question by a journalist who said this could happen if parents refuse to let their child identify as a cat.

Government officials argue this is not possible, since the bill sets a high threshold for an offence, requiring both abuse and serious harm as well as an attempt to change the person’s sexual orientation or gender identity.

Phillipson said: ‘This government is clear: we should live in a society that is tolerant, and that allows people to be their true selves without living in fear. That is the modern Britain I know.

‘For almost a decade, there has been political consensus and there has been international consensus that abusing someone to try and change their sexuality should be illegal.

‘Until now, that consensus has included Kemi Badenoch and much of the Conservative frontbench, who we now see pledged their support loudly and clearly.

‘In chasing Reform into the gutter, Badenoch’s Conservatives have shown their true colours: no interest in supporting LGBT+ people, no interest in calling out abuse of LGBT+ people, and no interest in a tolerant, modern Britain.’

Many of the Conservative objections to the bill were set out in a report by the Policy Exchange thinktank last week, including the idea that protections in the bill for people with non-binary identities could end up being so broad as to include those who are ‘catgender’, meaning they identify as cats.

Calling the bill an attack on people who do not share a ‘narrow set of beliefs about gender identity’, the report also argues that conversion practices are comparatively rare, and that any offences arising from those practices are already covered by existing laws.

A Conservative spokesperson said: ‘No one can accuse Kemi Badenoch of abandoning LGBT people. Years ago, against civil servants’ advice, she met Keira Bell, a young lesbian who had been prescribed puberty blockers and testosterone and later underwent a double mastectomy, treatment she came to regret.

‘Labour’s conversion practices bill risks criminalising the honest, exploratory conversations that young people like Keira should have before they are led towards life-changing surgery.

‘Proper protections for young LGBT people means ensuring they receive thoughtful support and clinical advice without pressure to reach a particular conclusion. That is why we are concerned about this bill and its implications for young people.’
output.standfirst: A draft law banning LGBT+ conversion practices, carrying jail terms of up to five years, remains open for consultation after the Conservatives withdrew support; Phillipson accused Badenoch of ‘no interest in supporting LGBT+ people’.
output.progress: The government’s draft bill to ban LGBT+ conversion practices remains open for public consultation, with potential jail terms of up to five years for abusers.

output.headline: Scarf seller who talks shoppers out of buying becomes Seoul’s biggest attraction
output.bodyHtml:
By mid-morning the main alley of Namdaemun market in Seoul is ringed by private security guards and police, and the queue – penned behind a cordon – shuffles forward clutching numbered tickets. Those in it, mostly middle-aged women, have waited more than an hour.

In front of them, a stall holder is selling scarves, offering a deal of six for 10,000 won (about $6.80), roughly $1.15 each. The salesman – who is known by nicknames such as “scarf ajeossi”, or scarf uncle – has become something of a national sensation for a sales technique that consists of talking customers out of purchases. “Don’t spend your money,” he quips. “It doesn’t suit you.”

The combination of his affectionate bluntness and amusing selling style – coupled with praise for his looks – has seen him become a huge star on social media, with customers and livestreamers flocking to the market and clips racking up millions of views online.

Lee Mi-hwa, who came from Yongin, about 35km south of Seoul, after seeing him on YouTube, says: “He’s really famous. He’s the hottest thing right now.”

Namdaemun is South Korea’s oldest and largest traditional market, a warren of alleys beside the old south gate that gives it its name, and a place long synonymous with the hard sell.

Passersby stop to ask whether a celebrity is inside due to all the commotion, while YouTubers try to get a glimpse of him, livestreaming the chaos.

The scarf seller does not publicise his real name, so nicknames fill the gap. As well as scarf uncle, there is “Scarfrio”, a playful mashup of scarf and Leonardo DiCaprio, in a nod to his looks and easy charm. “He’s so handsome,” says a woman in the queue.

Scarfrio is rugged rather than polished, dressed in a market trader’s layers for the autumn cold, and poses for selfies with his newfound fanbase.

That appeal has seen him go viral for his salesmanship and he has since opened Instagram and YouTube accounts, racking up millions of views.

On Wednesday, Lee Ji-hyun joined the queue at 10am and reached the front at 11.20am. “I finally got some,” she says excitedly, holding up her prize. “The way he talks is so lovely. A man like that deserves to do well, so I came to cheer him on, and I ended up buying.”

She had stood beside him long enough to hear the sales pitch. “Nothing worth seeing here,” he tells shoppers, and “come on, mum, dig underneath, dig underneath”, endearingly urging them to rummage through the pile of scarves. “He feels like my son, like a younger brother,” she says.

“This fabric is marvellous. Have you felt how soft it is? How is this 1,600 won?” she says. The packaging says made in China.

Police have been called in to usher his devotees out of the crowded alley as his popularity and the crowds have grown, and the scarf seller has had to shut up shop several times as a result. Private security was hired in early November to manage the hordes, and he has stopped announcing his opening hours.

But not everyone is amused. A few metres away, another stall holder, who has sold shoes at the market for more than 30 years, is unimpressed with the crowds that now spill across his shopfront.

“Business is bad. The passage next to me gets blocked and it’s really hard on me,” says the man, who gives his name only as Moon. “The wider area is fine, because the people come. It’s the shops nearby that take the damage.”

Young people film the scarf seller for YouTube and Instagram, he says, and come just to see his face. “This is pulling a lot of people in,” he says. “But there’s no spending.”

Bae Jong-min, who sells scarves next to Scarfrio’s stall, was more upbeat.

“There are a lot of people coming to the market, so for the market as a whole it’s a good thing,” he says, pointing to the restaurants, coffee shops and food stalls. “But I do worry about crowding issues.”

Scarfrio said days earlier on social media that the attention had left him carrying “enormous pressure and anxiety”, and he apologised to the traders around him.

Lee Ji-hyun, meanwhile, had not set foot in Namdaemun for 30 years, despite living in Seoul. “If I need something I go to the supermarket, I never thought about coming to this market,” she says. “I now plan to come once a month.”
output.standfirst: Known as Seoul’s ‘scarf uncle’, a Namdaemun market trader has become a South Korean sensation for a sales technique built on talking customers out of purchases, drawing queues, livestreamers and crowds so large that police and private security now help manage them
output.progress: Police and private security have been brought in to manage the crowds flocking to see him, after the scarf seller had to shut up shop several times.

output.headline: Extra funding keeps Poundland trading as rescue talks continue
output.bodyHtml:
Gordon Brothers, which is understood to be supportive of a further 10 working days’ grace for Poundland, has released £10m more in funds to help the retailer secure new stock and keep trading. Poundland’s directors are now seeking that extension, which must be approved by the high court.

MPs have accused the owner of Poundland of extracting millions of pounds from the budget retailer when it was on a “knife-edge” as it seeks extra time to secure a rescue deal.

The management of Poundland, which employs 12,000 people and operates 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, will seek a two-week extension of legal protection from creditors from the high court on Thursday morning.

The budget chain’s owner, Gordon Brothers, is under pressure to accept a bid for the company that would save retail jobs and protect thousands of suppliers. Poundland filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators two weeks ago.

Related: ‘I’d steal 10-15 times a day’: ex-offenders on the addictions driving prolific shoplifting

The legal measure protects Poundland from the demands of creditors until Thursday morning while a solution to its problems is sought.

Without the legal protection in place, Poundland is likely to have to call in administrators; the advisory firm Alix Partners is already lined up.

The European head of Gordon Brothers, Mark Newton-Jones, gave evidence in private for almost two hours to the Commons business select committee on Wednesday afternoon after MPs called on the government to protect Poundland and other high street stores from “predatory capitalism” and asset-stripping last week.

Liam Byrne, the chair of the committee, said that after questioning Newton-Jones he was “deeply concerned that Gordon Brothers’ behaviour may have jeopardised thousands of jobs on Britain’s high streets”.

He said: “Over the last 17 months, they have taken millions out of Poundland when the business was on a ‘knife-edge’.

“Now Poundland appears to be on the rebound, there’s concerning signs it’s been strangled of access to its own funds in what should be its busiest trading period in the run-up to Christmas.

“Worse, Gordon Brothers refused to say it will prioritise saving jobs over and above its own financial returns.”

The committee separately heard from Poundland’s management team, led by Barry Williams, who had been fighting to save the business.

Sources said Poundland continued to trade well, with sales up year on year, despite its problems, but it has only enough cash to support the business for a short period. Gordon Brothers has said Poundland remains “challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading”.

Gordon Brothers is understood to remain in talks with three potential bidders for the entire chain but has indicated it can raise more from a break-up of Poundland, selling off stock and parcels of stores to rival retailers.

The bids are understood to be worth less than the £30m in debts taken on by shareholders when Gordon Brothers bought the chain. It bought Poundland for a nominal £1 from its previous owner, the European retail group Pepco, in June 2025.

Pepco still holds £7.5m of the £30m shareholder debt. It is prepared to wait for repayment in the hope of saving the business.

Gordon Brothers is still in talks with Martin Property Group, the Northern Irish family-owned firm supporting a management-backed rescue bid for the discount chain, which includes the Dealz chain in Ireland.

Martin Property Group’s first bid had been rejected by Gordon Brothers as it amounted to no more than half the £30m it wants for Poundland with less than £7m up front.

A little-known finance company, Xyra Group, is thought to have offered about £12m up front and close to £30m in total. However, Xyra has not been involved with retail businesses previously.

Gordon Brothers has been approached for comment.
output.standfirst: Extra funding and a bid for more time at the high court aim to keep Poundland trading, as MPs accuse its owner of extracting millions from the chain while it was on a 'knife-edge'
output.progress: Gordon Brothers has released an extra £10m so Poundland can secure new stock and keep trading.

output.headline: Lost Roman leg recasts the story of empire’s reach into Scotland
output.bodyHtml:
A bronze leg dug from a bog in rural Scotland more than 200 years ago, then tucked away for a century in a duke’s storeroom, is now helping to rewrite the history of the Roman empire.

The so-called Mislington leg was long assumed by antiquarians to have been looted, perhaps from York, hacked off by marauding Scottish tribes and carried north over Hadrian’s Wall. “We cannot visualise the conditions which would have led to its erection anywhere north of the Great Wall,” the scholar James Curle said in 1932.

Archaeologists now believe the hefty gilded bronze limb instead came from the Scottish Borders, part of a vast statue of the emperor Antoninus Pius on horseback erected near Hawick after his armies took control of southern Scotland in about AD140.

Bearing significant similarities to imperial statues in other frontier regions, it is the centrepiece of the largest exhibition ever staged on the Romans in Scotland, which opens on Saturday at the National Museum of Scotland in Edinburgh.

It spent a century in the “charter room” at Dalkeith House near Edinburgh, one of the stately homes owned by the Duke of Buccleuch, after being dug up in 1820.

It is now displayed alongside other artefacts that the museum’s curators believe prove the Romans were a far more significant force north of Hadrian’s Wall than previously realised, occupying large areas of the country, producing new artworks and shaping the politics of Scotland long after they retreated.

Dr Fraser Hunter, principal curator of the exhibition, Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire, believes such statues would have had a profound impact on iron-age communities – and that, far from being hacked off, the leg was carefully removed and deposited where it was found 1,700 years later.

“These kind of things are not only visually dominant but they look really, really alien,” Hunter said. “There is effectively no naturalist art in the iron age – very, very little. The whole idea of depicting a person is absolutely alien to the iron-age worldview.”

Among a series of firsts, the exhibition also includes a new reconstruction of a heavily decorated earthenware bowl from Inveresk, east of Edinburgh. The village is the site of a large Roman fort and town that was, Hunter believes, a centre of imperial power during the Antonine period in Scotland of AD142 to 165 – the second of three periods of Roman occupation of Scotland.

Hunter estimates that about 10,000 troops, including auxiliaries from places such as modern-day Romania and north Africa, were stationed across southern and eastern Scotland, alongside perhaps another 10,000 camp followers, wives and enslaved people.

Bethany Simpson, an assistant curator, said the bowl displayed a unique combination of animal reliefs involving dolphins, stags and a stylised hunting dog. “You only find it in Inveresk. It’s not seen anywhere else in Scotland; it’s not seen anywhere in the UK,” she said.

The museum is also showing for the first time two remarkably well preserved, locally carved stone altars from a mithraeum excavated at Inveresk. The museum uses dramatic lighting to demonstrate the vibrant colours originally painted on them.

One has slits cut into its hollowed-out stone, radiating from the carved head of Mithras, with holes carved into its eyes and mouth to allow lamplight to shine out in the smoky darkness of the temple.

The show also includes the entire skeleton of a horse, carefully buried at Inveresk, which was also home to a small amphitheatre – a rare find in frontier towns. “The burial of cavalry horses in Britain is rare,” Hunter said. “Normally they just get disposed of, so this must have been a valued steed, which is really interesting.”

Related: What did the Romans ever give Scotland? Heated floors, flashy sandals, sun gods – and a lot of nails

The exhibition focuses on Rome’s influence on indigenous Celtic tribes, their culture and political structures. Recent scholarship suggests there was no tradition of carving in pre-Roman Scotland, but from the Roman occupation sprang rich native styles, leading to highly ornate Pictish standing stones.

Celtic rulers were beguiled by the silver used by the Romans for coins and jewellery; until then silver was unknown locally. The Romans used it to buy loyalty. Yet, by the third and fourth centuries, the Roman threat led the Pictish tribes to merge forces into an “anti-Roman coalition”.

“What Roman interventions effectively do is they create a worse enemy. It’s the problem that empires often have in dabbling around their edges,” Hunter said.

“So you get these larger-scale polities emerging. But they are also using Rome as a model, and the emergence of things like the Pictish symbols is absolutely tied into their exposure to sculpture and writing. So these are local responses to these kind of things, but in a highly creative, wonderfully magnificent manner.”
output.standfirst: Once dismissed as looted war booty, the gilded bronze limb is now understood to be part of a huge statue of Antoninus Pius – centrepiece of the biggest exhibition staged on Roman Scotland, opening in Edinburgh.
